utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Doctor. Good morning, everyone. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Excellencies. Good morning to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Dr. Nielsen.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. I wish you a productive morning. We cannot rest until we still have work to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We were talking about two unauthorised documents or perhaps even three documents. You established similarities between that document and the document dated 19 December 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] I take it you are referring to the two unauthored documents on the decentralisation of internal affairs and, yes, to some extent in my report I discuss similarities between those two documents and the December 19th document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You are familiar with the Defence thesis that those were benevolent proposals that came from the top echelons. Do you have anything to say with this regard in view of the fact that a recommendation in those documents was that our structures should adhere to the JNA and to resubordinate themselves to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I became familiar with that thesis through one of your earlier questions during my testimony, and I believe that I spoke of my view of that thesis. Again, it is clear that the Serbs working in the then-joint Bosnian MUP in the second half of 1991 viewed the JNA and indeed all organs of the federal Yugoslav government as organs that were -- to which they had an affiliation and were predisposed and from whom they could seek assistance if that became necessary in light of a deteriorating security situation. So it is quite logical with -- to me and I agree with you that they -- these documents contemplate co-operation between the police and the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. With regard to the organigramme, did you find the document that was final and that was finally adopted? Do we have a document in lieu of that draft document?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure which particular document you are referring to and whether I found a final version of that document. All of the documents to which I have just referred are, as far as I can see, draft documents. These two on the decentralisation or possibility of decentralisation of affairs in Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, as I note in the report, for example on page 21, one of these documents pushes for the establishment of a new CSB in Trebinje and that was indeed something that came about through the adoption of a new Law on Internal Affairs by the Bosnian Serbs subsequently. That is one of many examples from these documents where I see that the contemplations contained in those documents later become reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, do you agree with me that final documents should have more weight than drafts, because any draft is subject to changes?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. I agree that final versions of these documents would have more weight than drafts. Unfortunately, those final versions, if they exist, were not available. I did not find them in the extensive searches I made of archives related to the Bosnian Serb police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree with me that you said that on the 16th of April, Minister Subotic proclaimed a state of an imminent threat of war? Do you agree that the Muslim side did that on the 8th of April, which was eight days earlier?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I note both the 8th of April decision as well as, I believe, Subotic's decision or relevant decisions of the RS government on the proclamation of an imminent threat of war in paragraphs 189 and 190 of my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that the Muslim side -- or, rather, that Alija Izetbegovic proclaimed general mobilisation on the 4th of April, contrary to the wishes of Professor Plavsic and Professor Koljevic, the Serbian members of the Assembly who opposed that decision?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that fact and I note in my report that partly out of -- as a result of that disagreement, Plavsic and Koljevic resigned and that is in footnote 188.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree with me that when general mobilisation is proclaimed one has to assume that there is an enemy out there? What did Mr. Izetbegovic assume who his enemy was? Do you agree that that was aimed primarily against the Bosnian Serbs and only later against the JNA?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that a general mobilisation normally takes place when there is some kind of security threat, internal or external, that gives cause for such a mobilisation. As to who Mr. Izetbegovic assumed his enemy was, I believe that is a question that is best addressed to those persons who were around Mr. Izetbegovic at that period in time since he is no longer available to answer that question. And I agree that at this point in time, as far as I know and not being an expert on the Bosnian Muslim political agenda at this time, I agree that Mr. Izetbegovic, as far as I know at this point, still had hope that the JNA would be a factor of stability in Bosnia and Herzegovina, whereas I believe he regarded some Bosnian Serb formations such as paramilitary formations with a more critical eye.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic is kindly asked to come closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you come closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The microphone will come closer to me in this particular instance. We have a saying, a proverb to that effect in our language. Do you remember that Mr. Izetbegovic proclaimed the state of war on the 20th or the 22nd of June? I believe that it was on the 20th of June. He proclaimed a state of war, and then he marked his enemies. In addition to the Bosnian Serbs, those were also Serbia and Montenegro. Those two states were marked as his enemies.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a subject which, in some respects, transcends my expertise. As far as I recall and I do not consider myself an expert on that subject, I do believe you're correct in stating that a state of war was proclaimed by Izetbegovic in June. However, I thought that I recalled that Mr. Izetbegovic was not declaring war against the Bosnian Serbs per se and that indeed there were at least some pronouncements during that period by the Bosnian government that Serbs would be welcome to assist them in defending Bosnia and Herzegovina as indeed some Serbs, for example, Jovan Divjak, did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: An exception that actually proves the rule.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree that Mr. Divjak is a very exceptional person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: An exceptional example as well; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In every sense of the word.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were an investigator from 2002 to 2004. You know that investigations also involved the cases of Izetbegovic and Tudjman; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will briefly respond in Serbian. [Interpretation] I believe that here there is a -- it is very important to make a distinction between an investigator and a researcher. I've always been a researcher, not an investigator, and I know that there were investigations carried out against Izetbegovic and Tudjman, but I personally did not participate in those investigations either as an analyst or a researcher.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, you did participate in interviewing some of the witnesses; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes. I participated in interviewing some witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You also read Stanisic's statement, and Stanisic provided his statement as a suspect; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I -- well, I should say I did not read Mico Stanisic's statement. I watched it on video because I was provided by the Prosecution in that case with the DVDs of his suspect interview prior to my testimony in that case, and I was very content to see that Mico Stanisic had read and agreed with significant portions of my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you review the materials relative to the responsibility of Izetbegovic and President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was certainly able to see some of the materials that were being used by the researchers who were working on Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat cases, particularly where such documents discussed, for example, co-operation between the Bosnian Serbs and the Bosnian Croats during the war in various instances. However, I did not review at any length that documentation, as my full-time job was reviewing the very large quantities of information related to the Bosnian Serb police and the police in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You studied the police in Serbia. Did you observe major antagonisms and mutual slandering between the federal SUP and the MUP of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I studied that subject. I am familiar with those major antagonisms which culminated in the forcible takeover of the Federal Secretariat for Internal Affairs by the MUP of Serbia in the fall of, I believe, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you will also agree that one group speaks of the other, one should take those words with some reservations.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree, and that is an excellent point. That is precisely why the vast majority of the documents that I cite in my report are documents produced by the Bosnian Serbs themselves so that I was not relying on potentially slanderous statements made by Bosnian Muslims or Bosnian Croats about the Bosnian Serbs, rather, I was interested in seeing how the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the RS looked seen with their own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You did not study the Muslim and Croat MUP. Did any of your colleagues study the conduct, the structure, and the essence of the MUP of what we call the Muslim-Croat federation? In other words, the remainder of the MUP of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, every man has only one life, and I could only study a limited amount of material, and so to my great regret I did not have time to study also the other MUPs in the former Yugoslavia, and precisely for that reason we had that division of labour to which I've earlier referred in the leadership research team. And indeed, I had colleagues who studied the structure and the essence of the organs of internal affairs, both in the entity known as Herceg-Bosna, as well as in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as well as the other entities or Ministries of Internal Affairs outside the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, for example Croatian MUP, RSK MUP, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you perhaps tell us who studied the Muslim part of the MUP in the same way you did with the Serbian part of the MUP, and have you ever seen the resulting materials?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Should I respond, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How is this relevant?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellency, if we describe the actions of only one boxer in the ring and the other is invisible, then the one whom we are describing looks ridiculous. We should actually see what the other side did and how that reflected on the activities of the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Doctor, you're not minded, you may not. I'll leave it in your hands.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I will again state that there were analysts who were working at the same time as I was, employed by the leadership research team and who were tasked to look at the MUP of Bosnia and Herzegovina and also tasked to look at the other MUPs. If -- if you would like and if the Chamber feels that it's relevant, I can put names to the analysts who were thus employed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, we don't think that that's relevant, and the witness doesn't need to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Defence will request all the materials directly from the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Since we don't have much time, Dr. Nielsen, we now have to draw your attention, we have to focus on the public security station's segment. I'm sure you'll agree with me that was the lowest-ranking organisational police unit in our regions; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: With great respect, please allow me to supplement your knowledge of the MUP. I would note that the public security station is the municipal level of the police in the organs of internal affairs, and there actually is another tier of the police hierarchy below the public security station, namely the police stations, "stanica milicije," that were at the local level, at the village level, often.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have that abbreviation for that police station? "Stanica milicije".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. During the period from November 1990 until the end of 1993, such police stations, at least in areas controlled by the Bosnian Serbs, were known as "stanice milicije" or SM as an abbreviation. After that, and I think this is important since there's a period of this case that goes into 1994 and 1995, they changed the word "milicija" to "policija" and therefore these became "policijska stanica," abbreviated PS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now look at 65 ter 15699 in e-court. Do you remember if you've ever seen this document? This was issued by the public security station in the municipality Centar in Sarajevo. The second paragraph describes a paramilitary formation which was brought by a local man from Apatin in Vojvodina. They styled themselves Chetniks and then they started bringing in people. They even brought in and arrested Mr. Petrovic, who was the president of the municipality and that was on the 6th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with this document, and it is exemplary of a trend of similar incidents during this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The public security station wrote to the ministry -- or, rather, to the Romanija Birac CSB to inform them what was going on. Can we go to the following page. This document should have a translation, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm afraid not. It's coming, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the first page. It says here that an individual went to Apatin in Vojvodina and brought back some men. Then they established themselves as a unit and then they started acting of their own will and the MUP informs their superiors that their conduct is out of order; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I would point out this is being filed by SJB Centar Sarajevo pursuant to an order issued on the 25th of July, 1992, which is this very period when the MUP is trying to crack down on such paramilitary formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Next page, please. Here we see that there are some percentages relating to the MUP, which indicate that the manpower has not been reached. It only has 30 per cent of the active-duty officers, and even such a low percentage are being asked to take part in combat. Would you agree that 30 per cent of manpower strength is not even enough to maintain law and order, let alone to send them to fight on the front line.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was definitely the subject of the constant complaints of this SJB as well as other SJBs at the time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, look at this page in English, and in Serbian it says that problems are caused by members -- individual members of the reserve force, and it says now that guarding of prisoners, expelled persons, et cetera. They said that they managed to reach an agreement with the SJB Vogosca and Pale to hand over such persons to them to be guarded. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is another significant topic dealt with in this document. I would note that all of the subjects are being dealt with pursuant to the 11 July 1992 meeting of the leadership of the RS MUP in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we have the next page in both languages, please, the last paragraph in Serbian where it reads that there are no military judiciary organs, and there are no department of military police or military prosecutors' offices. In English that's the second paragraph from the top. And before that, on the very top it says that it is difficult to maintain law and order, to control crime rates, to set up joint control and check-points for the prevention of looting, et cetera. And you couldn't expect 30 per cent of the police officers to do more than that, would you?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the conclusion of the police, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1558, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm going to skip some elements that are not encompassed by the indictment due to the lack of time. Can we now briefly look at 52881. I believe you also made reference to this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Number again?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's P281 -- 2881, or 65 ter 8106.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall this document?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If you agree, it seems that they are talking here about 54 criminal reports filed against Serbs, which means that 70 people were charged and that we have among them returnees, nine of them. There are 12 juveniles, of which 12 are Muslim, four are Roma, and a little bit down there you see that there are charges against violent crimes and sexual assaults.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic please slow down when citing figures. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: They couldn't follow. Please slow down when you cite figures.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So on page 1 it says that reports were filed for a total of 78 crimes. Seventy people were involved. Nine of them are returnees, 12 of them are juveniles, of which 12 are Muslim and 4 are Roma, which should make a total of 16. Do you agree that this breakdown shows that there were returnees already and that they are causing problems and that of the 70 criminal reports filed, 16 are against other ethnicities, whereas the remaining ones are against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that that is what the document states. I would also point out that statistics that are being collected and collated and published during this period should be taken with a grain of salt because particularly for persons of Muslim and Croat ethnicity, the police documentation also shows that very considerable numbers of them were being detained without any criminal complaints, and therefore statistics that are solely focused on criminal complaints or reports only show us part of the picture of what the police is engaged in during this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I would ask for the time to be allocated to the Prosecution to be allocated to me instead, because I'm going to ask you about this. So we have a fact that cannot be disputed, that we have 54 Serbs who were charged and only 16 others.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that this is what the document states.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said in your statement that by mid-June only six non-Serbs, mainly Muslims, remained in the MUP. Did you mean by that that there were six of them in the MUP headquarters, or did you have the entire structure of the MUP of Republika Srpska in mind?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document that I cite, and I'm trying to locate it right now, left me with the clear impression that that figure of six non-Serbs who were employed as of that point in time in the RS Ministry of Internal Affairs was a figure for the ministry as a whole and not for a particular regional centre or municipal police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, in the Stanisic and Zupljanin case, on page 5535, 26th of January, 2010, you accepted that at least another 140 employees, non-Serb employees, were in the MUP as a whole. Do you agree that this shouldn't be a final number? Do you recall that testimony? 26th of January, 2010, page 5535.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Now that you mention it, I do vaguely recall that exchange during my testimony in Stanisic and Zupljanin. I would again state that I was operating at the time with the knowledge that was in the documents that I was able to review, and as you point out, I corrected my view on that point in light of documents I believe produced by the Defence in the other case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that you saw for yourself and you confirmed that in your statements and your reports that Zupljanin permanently tried to preserve the multi-ethnic nature of the MUP in the region of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree as I did during my testimony during -- or in Stanisic and Zupljanin that there are documents, a number of documents in which Zupljanin tried, or at least asserted that he was trying to preserve the multi-ethnic nature of the MUP in the region of CSB Banja Luka. However, as I also note extensively in my report and in my testimony in Stanisic and Zupljanin, the overwhelming bulk of documentation from the area of CSB Banja Luka shows that that multi-ethnic nature was not preserved and indeed many of the persons subordinate to Mr. Zupljanin were actively engaged in preventing police officers of Muslim and Croat ethnicity from remaining in the MUP at that time, and I deal with that on pages 55 and subsequently of my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If we have time, we'll get back to this. 1D3631 in e-court. If necessary, can we please rotate the page. I believe we don't need a translation. There is a translation, though, but probably this will be sufficient since you can read the Cyrillic script. Is this a payroll list for August 1992, which says that only 50 per cent of salaries are payable? It says, "Authorised employees, former employees," and it says, Husein Rahmanovic, a Muslim; Saban Mujkic, a Muslim; Hadzan Bardak, a Muslim; Vehid Alihodzic, Muslim. Do you agree that all of these people that appear on this first page are all Muslims? And we also have another name, Husein Rahmanovic, the fourth from the top whose name is not underlined?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: A couple of points. I agree this appears to be a payroll list for August 1992. I do not necessarily see that it is a police payroll. I would note it also says that these are old employees. "Zastare radnike," it indicates at the top, whatever that may mean. I would then also very briefly note for the Court's information that the reference to the document stating that only six Muslim employees could be found in all of RS MUP is in paragraph 208 of my report. And specifically with respect to your previous question on CSB Banja Luka and the multi-ethnic character of the police in that area, I note in paragraph 195 that a report of CSB Banja Luka filed in August 1992 stated that all members of non-Serbian ethnicity had left the police and, in fact, a team of RS MUP that visited the public security station in Banja Luka said that the few remaining Bosnian Muslim employees had been put on leave. No one knew what to do with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Next page, please, so that we can see the stamp of Bijeljina MUP. This is the stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you go back to the first page? I wonder whether you answered the question whether all the names on this page are Muslims.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. The answer to that question is there are a number of names on this list that appear to be those of Muslims. There are also names of persons who are, it appears, of Serbian ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But those four, Husein, Saban, Hadzan, and Vehid, are all Muslims; right? The fourth name, the fifth name, the tenth and the eleventh name.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that those are all Muslim names and I would note that three of those four names are underlined.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we look at the stamp, and then we'll move to the next page. Republika Srpska, Ministry of the Interior, Bijeljina CSB; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, my reading of it is that it says Centre of Public Security in Bijeljina, which would indicate that this document would have to be -- or at least the stamp on the document is from after January 1994. [Interpretation] Public security centres and such centres did not exist back in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But this is August 1992. I don't know if it is a public security station or -- or a centre. So we have public and state security, and this refers to public security sector that these people worked in.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The word that I see here is "centre" and then "public security." This is what I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have the next page, please. Mulasalihovic, Dzevdet; Muhamed Krainovic. They're all Muslims as well, would you agree?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] yes, I agree, and I would again note that both Muhamed and Dzevdet are underlined.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we move two pages forward, please. Esref Aljic; Hrustem Hrustanbegovic [phoen]; Petar Bekter, probably a Croat; and Halid Halilic; and Mustafa Hamidovic. So we have four Muslims and one Croat on this list --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- do you agree?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you say "yes"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we move now four pages forward. Do you agree that Nermina Uzunic is a Muslim woman; Maida Arapovic; Radica Muhamedbegovic could be a Serb married to a Muslim, and that these are again Muslim names; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Nermina, Maida, and Radica are all females, probably working in the administration department; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree. RS MUP was not an equal opportunity work-force as regards gender.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted. But briefly can we show the English version for the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we have been following. This will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1559, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we now look at 65 ter 05672. Can we have the previous page in Serbian, please. Do you agree that here in the English -- can we have page 1 in the Serbian, please. And the next page in English. Please look where it says: "During 1992, between the 1st of January and the 20th of December, 1992, in the area of Banja Luka Public Security Station, the total of 107 violent crimes have been registered, 90 of which have been solved, which makes 84.1 per cent." Have you ever seen this report before?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree that that is what the document states, and yes, I have seen this document previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There is 12 juveniles among those 20, et cetera. Can we look at the next page in Serbian so that we can see the table. Look at the table, and the last paragraph which reads that regardless of the inter-ethnic conflicts, as far as the perpetrators and the victims of violent crimes are concerned, it corresponds to the make-up of the population, ethnic make-up of the population, and it says that most often the attackers and victims are of the same ethnicity. The most numerous among them are Serbs, 74 of them, actually, which is 73 per cent, 8 Croats, and 19 Muslims. The similar situation is among victims: Of a total of 122 victims, 69 were Serbs, which makes 58 per cent, 16 Croats, et cetera. You have seen this document?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As previously noted, I have seen this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you say that 84 per cent of solved cases during wartime could be described as a quite remarkable achievement by the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is certainly a very high percentage. However, as I also noted this morning with respect to a similar document, I as an analyst take all such statistics, both the total incidence of crimes and the distribution of perpetrators and victims during this period, with a rather enormous grain of salt, because there are a lot of things that are changing, and as the police themselves admit in other documents, a lot of crime that is not being documented, as well as persons who are being detained without being charged. So this document, however thorough it may appear at first glance, paints only part of larger picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we have the next page in English so that the Chamber and the Prosecution can look at these figures, although you can see them in this table. But do you agree that on page 1 there is a remark that this is an official secret which is strictly confidential for -- only for the eyes of the minister, so it's not intended for public use? Next page, please. So we have numbers here. So the Serbs constitute the largest number of both perpetrators and victims. Slightly more of them are Muslim, and the Croats constitute the lowest number, which exactly reflects the ethnic make-up of the population. Here it says that in most cases, both the perpetrators and the victims are Serbs, for example, which says that in most cases we have people committing crimes within their own ethnic group. Now let's look at page 1 so that we can verify that this was an official secret and a strictly confidential document.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that this document is a strictly confidential document that was, as you say, not produced for the media, but, rather, produced for the internal consumption of employees and managers of the Ministry of Internal Affairs. I would again point out that when we talk about anything reflecting the ethnic make-up of the population during this period, it is important to remember that the ethnic composition of the population in Banja Luka, as in so many other municipalities during this period, was not static but was rapidly changing due to the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1560, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we now see 65 ter 06732. Do you agree that this report was drafted based on a decision of the CSB Banja Luka, dated 14 August. The commission had inspected public security stations in Prijedor, Bosanski Novi, and Sanski Most and a report was compiled. Reference is made to collection centres in the first paragraph. The document originates from Bosanski Novi and the collection centre in question is also Bosanski Novi. In the middle part of the first paragraph we read however: These activities did not have the desired effect on the voluntary relinquishment of arms and apart from that, during the night of 10 May, 1992, in the village of Blagaj Rijeka, according to the report of a military police patrol an attack was mounted upon it. These events provoked a series of attacks on the areas and villages with majority Muslim populations. Thus on 24 May 1992, the entire population from the villages in the area of Dolina, Japra, Japra Valley was accommodated in the central part of Blagaj Japra. Towards the end of the first paragraph, it says Territorial Defence units or combat units of the JNA participated in the -- those battles. It says here all these attacks were carried out by armed and uniformed persons who self-organised or members of Territorial Defence units or combat units of the JNA but members or employees of the Bosanski Novi public security station did not take part in these attacks. Do you remember this report?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have reviewed this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt Mr. Karadzic but this report from the Bosanski Novi SJB is contained within the Defence exhibit D00470, which is the bigger report about Sanski Most, Bosanski Novi and Prijedor, so I don't know whether we want to be going to the exhibit so that we don't have a duplication of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Should we upload the 447 and take a look.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's 470 -- D470, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: D470, yes. That's probably that. Can we go to the following page?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's on page 17 of the English and page 13 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could please all unnecessary microphones be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This was a description of what was going on. It says here that uncontrolled groups and units. And then can we go to the following page in Serbian. No. This is not the same, no. This is not the same in the Serbian version. This is not an identical document. The English version seems to be identical, but the Serbian is not. Can we also look at the following English page. Maybe we will be able to get our bearings. This is Sanski Most, what we see in Serbian. Can we get the next English page. Okay. Do you agree that from the 2nd of June, 1992, the forces beyond control retaliated against the Muslims and attacked their property? Three hundred persons, mostly of Muslim ethnicity were brought in. They -- most of them were of military age, and they were accommodated in a collection centre that was disbanded on the 5th of June. Some 17 people who were considered to be of security interest were detained on the premises of the military police, whereas the others were allowed to go home. Do you remember this report?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. I -- it's on page 23 of this document, the B/C/S, for the Bosanski Novi. The -- in my haste, I saw Bosanski Novi, but that was the actual commissioner's report about Novi, but the SJB report is on page 23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, this is okay. We can see the document. Can we now look at two pages further ahead. Do you remember, Dr. Nielsen, that the military and the police were arguing on who's supposed to guard the evacuated population, who is supposed to guard those who were arrested, and what about -- and who was supposed to guard those who were detained? There was an argument between the two institutions about that; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the subject of protracted disagreement between the army and the police, and it was one of the topics discussed at length at the 11 July 1992 meeting in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the police wanted to guard only those that were being investigated, those that were possibly subject to criminal proceedings, and the police mainly succeeded in that attempt? They were also of the opinion that the military should guard prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that that is what the police wanted to do. However, until approximately the end of August 1992, they were unsuccessful in restricting themselves to that narrower type of activity, but they did certainly push for that starting in the second half of July and going into August. I think I've referred elsewhere to them trying to divest themselves of the business of operating or guarding detention facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that our language makes a distinction between a person who is arrested and the person who is detained, that a person who is arrested is subject possibly to criminal proceedings, whereas a detainee or a prisoner of war is somebody who was captured during fighting a -- and does not necessarily have to be subject to criminal proceedings?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I agree that that distinction exists.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So if we find a document containing the word "prisoner," we should investigate whether that prisoner is a possible subject to criminal proceedings or a prisoner of war. In other words, that a distinction should be made between a detainee, meaning a prisoner of war, and a prisoner.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that there is a difference between a prisoner of war and a prisoner such as the type of person who might be incarcerated in a penal institution, and there is a difference which is also reflected in the police documentation between prisoners or prisoners of war and those who are merely detained. I would point out that as so many other aspects, and we discussed this yesterday, the police were not always extremely attentive to precision in terminology in their own documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just for the record, your answer to the previous question was in the positive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That distinction exists in the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that Keraterm and Omarska were investigation centres, and wherever the police stood guard, one would also find investigators, investigating judges, because those were the places where investigations and interviews were taking place, and the triage of those who were detained there. Manjaca, on the other hand, was a prisoner of war camp that was established by the former JNA even before the war in Bosnia started?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that Manjaca was a prisoner of war camp and that's what I call it in paragraph 288 of my report. I also agree that it was a different from Keraterm, Trnopolje, and Omarska. Whereas Manjaca was operated by the army of the RS, the VRS, the other facilities were primarily operated by the police. In Omarska's case, pursuant to the orders of the Crisis Staff in Prijedor. And I would also agree that the police characterised Omarska and Keraterm not necessarily as investigation centres. Sometimes they called them reception centres, "prihvatni centri," but I would note that the interrogation of persons in all facilities often was conducted through teams consisting of military, public security, and national security officials as indicated in paragraph 288.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you notice that, for example, after those investigative actions, in Prijedor from Omarska and Keraterm people were released because they did not pose a security threat? Fifty-nine per cent were released and 41 were forwarded to Manjaca as prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not familiar with that precise figure. I would note that in paragraph 289 of my report, a number of these facilities is dealt with and the police statistics show that 8.660 informational interviews had been conducted with 5.740 persons during this period of the summer of 1992. However, only four criminal complaints were filed based on these. I also do not know where the persons to whom you refer as being released from Omarska and Keraterm were released to. In any case, I believe they were not permitted to return to their previous residences.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, Dr. Nielsen, we have proof that they themselves wanted to go to Trnopolje because they thought that they would feel safe there. They did not want to return home, because they couldn't get police protection there. There simply was not enough police officers. Do you know that Trnopolje was a camp established by prisoners themselves?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That description of Trnopolje does not conform to the descriptions of Trnopolje that I find in the police documentation. I also do not have the information from the documentation that I examined to be able to conclude or agree with you that prisoners -- or, excuse me, detainees who had been in Omarska and Keraterm voluntarily went to Trnopolje. I do, however, have information in the report, including, for example, reports by Vinko Kondic, who was the chief of police in Kljuc, stating that the atmosphere in his and other municipalities in Bosnian Krajina was such that Muslims who tried to return to their own homes were not safe and were in many cases attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we now see 65 ter 05440. I have to skip quite a number of documents unless I'm given more time in the next session. Maybe this is food for thought. Maybe the next session could be split between the Prosecutor and Defence. I have to deal with the special unit, because you yourself mentioned that unit in your report. Are you familiar with this document issued on the 6th of May, 1992? And in this document a reference is made to a special line-up involving a newly established detachment of special purpose police.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that you are referring -- well, actually, I'm not sure whether you're referring to the unit led by Karisik or whether you're referring to the unit in CSB Banja Luka where, indeed, on the favourite holiday of the police, Security Day, there was such a parade, in which I believe you and other leaders of the Bosnian Serb leadership were in attendance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The day before that there was an Assembly session where I took my duties. That was on the 12th of May. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we go to the following page. We are interested in what the objectives of that event were. In English, I suppose we have to go a page further ahead, and in Serbian, it is the last page. It says here: "I draw your attention to the expectations from this event, which is to present our forces and the determination of the police to preserve public peace and order, in the current very complex situation. It is necessary that you make these preparations with utmost responsibility ...," and so on and so forth. Do you agree that the main task given to this unit was to preserve public peace and order? Right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree that that was the main task given to this unit, which was somewhat ironic given that documentation by the police from around the same period, as I note in -- or statements by the police in the same period, as I note in paragraph 224, indicated that the chief of the sector for crime in CSB Banja Luka was aware that that unit, which had paramilitary origins, included some persons who may have committed criminal acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. In the course of 1992, they were established and disbanded. That's what we established yesterday, that they were disbanded for the reasons explained by yourself, because it -- it was impossible to trust the legal conduct of those people.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. This unit which was given the main task of preserving public peace and order was, in fact, disbanded in August 1992, precisely because its conduct was not contributing to the preservation of public peace and order, but, rather, producing a contrary effect, in the view of the Bosnian Serb Ministry of Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that Stojan Zupljanin participated in the event and said that he was proud that many Muslims and Croats had remained with us and that 50.000 citizens of Banja Luka applauded him by way of supporting that multi-ethnic composition of the force? We saw the clip here, and we -- it was admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not familiar with that particular clip, but, yes, I certainly am familiar with the fact that Stojan Zupljanin participated in that event and spoke of the security situation in Bosnian Krajina and that he, as I noted previously, at this point was making public statements asserting that the purpose of the police in the CSB Banja Luka region would be to maintain representation for all the ethnic communities of Bosnian Krajina. And he also, as I note in paragraph 194, at around this same time insisted that he wanted to keep a national representation in the police, that is, proportionate to the national structure of the population in those municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1561, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we now see 65 ter 05537. Do you agree that this document was issued on the 21st of July? It is a report on some unknown people presenting themselves in front of Dusan Djukic's house, which at the time was inhabited by the family of Amir Durgutovic. The house was attacked. Amir fled. They opened fire after him. After that, Amir Durgutovic, a Muslim, found an official ID of a member of the special unit and took it to the public security station in Banja Luka and reported the incident and also the men in question. Can we go to the following page? It says here that there were four men involved, members of the detachment for special purposes, and a criminal report was filed against all of them. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I agree this is one of a number of incidents where we see that persons of Bosnian Serb ethnicity who were harbouring and protecting persons of Muslim ethnicity, for example, were themselves subjected to attacks or assaults, unfortunately, in some cases, as in the present case, by members of RS MUP. In this case, members of the Special Police detachment of CSB Banja Luka, which was subordinate to Zupljanin. A number of such incidents took place, which led, as you note, to criminal complaints against these persons, and as I deal with it in paragraph 226 of my report, when two members of this unit were finally arrested, the unit in fact launched a -- basically, an armed assault against the prison in Banja Luka, threatening that they would actually attack the prison if the members of that unit were not arrested -- or, excuse me, released. This is an incident which contributed to the tension between Tutus and Zupljanin, because Tutus felt that Zupljanin was taking the side of those officers who had been arrested by the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, soon thereafter, two or three weeks after this incident, the unit was disbanded; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, although a number of the personnel who had been suspected of engaging in criminal activity during their period of employment for the CSB Banja Luka Special Police Unit continued to work in the RS MUP. Indeed, some of them were promoted, such as Ljuban Ecim who occupied several positions in the National Security Service of the RS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, we established yesterday that part of the campaign against Ljuban Ecim was slander, gossip, Serbia's favourite pastime; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I do not wish to agree with you about what Serbia's favourite -- or the Serbs' favourite pastime is. I would hope it would be tennis now. But I would state that as regards this incident, certainly Vladimir Tutus whom, as you know, is, himself, a Serb, he complained that such incidents were damaging the rule of law in the RS and, as I note in paragraph 226, he stated specifically with respect to such incidents and I quote, "The state cannot be built on violence." As for Mr. Ecim, I think his subsequent activities, including his very large role in narcotics trafficking in the Balkans speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I note the time. It's time to take a break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please reconsider sharing the next session with the Prosecution. Can I get part of the time that the Prosecution needed so that I can deal at least with a few more topics? And I kindly ask that this document be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1562, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the Chamber will give you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: A quarter of an hour to conclude your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will resume at five past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we briefly have a look at 65 ter 5534. 05534. I think it's what we had already. Actually, I thought it was somewhat different. Well, all right. Let us just remind ourselves of this. It's been admitted. Committed a crime. On the 21st this criminal report is being written up, and the centre of security services is being informed. It's the public security station that is informing the security services centre, and since this has already been admitted, can we have 65 ter 1595. Let's just draw your attention to the dates. Let us all pay attention to the dates. This is the 21st of July. 65 ter 1595. Can we have that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. 65 ter 5540 is identical to 5534?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You said 5534. What was uploaded was 5540.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is a new document now. Yes. This one hasn't been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So do you agree -- ah-ha. I see. 1595, this is what we see in Serbian now --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before the break, Mr. Karadzic took the witness to 05537, and that was admitted as D1562. He then called up 05534 and we thought that was the same document as the previous one, but it's in fact different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we upload 5534 first, let us see what ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I look at the Serbian version, it seems to be what we already had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. It is the Prosecution Exhibit P2770.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have 65 ter 1595.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Exhibit D1534, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that in the first paragraph here it says already on the 27th of July, that is to say, six days after what had happened, the minister issued an order to disband these units, all of these units, that belonged to the public security stations here, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you dealt with it yesterday, and we admitted it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I would like to say:

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree, Dr. Nielsen, you mentioned that during the examination-in-chief, do you agree that this does not mean that the proceedings were stopped?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Proceedings against whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It means that the units were disbanded. They were resubordinated to the army. They were sent to the army. However, proceedings against the perpetrators of crimes were not halted or stayed in that way; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the case that the proceedings were not abandoned. However, as I pointed out yesterday, and as has been confirmed to me repeatedly by my very close colleagues in the RS MUP, most of such -- of -- of these proceedings against police officers languished in various desk drawers for the duration of the war and only afterwards became the process of vigorous prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in view of the time we have, I would like to ask you the following: You mentioned that Muslims in Banja Luka were being dismissed and that they left the police and so on. Do you remember that all of these recommendations were actually made orally for their own safety and nothing was done in writing to dismiss them unless they left the territory and stopped coming to work? You spoke about that on page 38 of the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a subject that I deal with at length in my report. I note that members of the police in areas that came under the control of the RS MUP were ordered to sign or swear solemn oaths to the MUP. In many cases, Muslims and Croats did not wish to take those oaths. In some cases, they were not even allowed to take such oaths. I'm not aware of the fact that the police of Croat or Muslim ethnicity in the RS MUP voluntarily left based on oral recommendations that that was for their own safety. I don't find a reflection of that in the documentation. And as I note again in paragraph 195, certainly in Banja Luka Public Security Station, the few remaining Bosnian Muslim employees were put on leave because no one knew what to do with them. This seems to contradict assertions made by Zupljanin and others that Bosnian Serbs and Bosnian Croats would be welcome in the ranks of the RS MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Nielsen, did you see a single dismissal in writing except in cases when people were away for a long time, which meant that a particular policeman had left the area? Did you see a single notice that was made on ethnic grounds?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is in fact the case that I do not recall seeing notices of termination of employment that were solely made on ethnic grounds. The dramatic change in the ethnic demographics of the police that took place in the RS MUP in this period was largely accomplished without such termination orders being issued. There were many other ways in which it was made known to Muslims and Croats that they were not welcome as employees in the RS MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, we have no proof of that; right? It's an assumption.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree with that. I would again, for example, point out that there were municipalities in which Muslims and Croats were not permitted to swear the solemn oath. Even in those isolated cases, and they were isolated cases in which they actually did wish to swear an oath to a Serbian Ministry of Internal Affairs. And I would point out even with the caveat of the document that you raised earlier that certainly the RS MUP's own documentation when taken in its totality clearly reflects that Muslims and Croats were largely removed from the ranks of the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the RS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We don't have time, Dr. Nielsen, to prove that, so we have to challenge it this way. However, we'll deal with it some other time. On page 49, you deal with the topic of Tajfun or Sigma. I am going to put something to you and you are going to agree or disagree with that assumption. Tajfun was an intelligence group in the JNA that got in touch with us, and since before the war the JNA -- the JNA was hostile towards us. We accepted their information; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the interests of time, I will agree with that statement, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Further on during the first months of the war, they continued working as an intelligence service, and when they started bringing people into custody, I ordered Mr. Stanisic to integrate them in state security but not as a group but as individuals, rather. Do you have that information?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with the rough outlines of that statement, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Afterwards, they were reluctant to be resubordinated, and they continued to exist as a group. Afterwards, Tomo Kovac suggested that they be arrested and that was approved, and indeed they were arrested; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct that the members of Tajfun were reluctant to be resubordinated, and yes, it is correct that - and now we're well past 1992 - they were the subject of attempts to arrest and disband that group.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's right. Now, furthermore, do you agree that already in April or perhaps even before that, in 1994, I think -- or, actually, 1993, they sent anonymous information to the state security of Serbia and ultimately they deceived the state security of Serbia when they said that I had given them approval to co-operate with the DB of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm very thankful as an analyst to get this additional information from you, because it was, indeed, my conjecture based on the documentation available to me about Tajfun that certainly they did send anonymous information to the State Security Service of Serbia, much of which cast the activities of various organs of the Republika Srpska in a critical or negative light, and I was always very suspicious because of the efforts made by the RS leadership to eliminate Tajfun, that members of that same group should have obtained your permission to once again engage in similar activities under the auspices of the State Security Service of Serbia, although they of course, as you say, deceived Belgrade in stating that they had received such authorisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, it's just a question of the sequence of events. My proposition is that first we asked for them to be resubordinated. Then we asked for them to be banned, and then we ordered their arrest, and it was only then that they started writing about this alleged corruption of the leadership of Republika Srpska. So first we banned them, and then they started slandering us in Serbia. And do you remember that that was at the time when our relations with the leadership, the political leadership, of Serbia were very chilled and ultimately broken off altogether?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly agree that the writings of this group, the dispatches of this group, which in large part focussed on allegations of corruption in the leadership of Republika Srpska and in the families of various members of the leadership of Republika Srpska was unacceptable -- or were unacceptable to the RS leadership, and that, would say, strengthened the resolve of the RS leadership to ban this organisation. It may also have strengthened the resolve of members of that organisation to augment their reporting on such activities. At any case, it's clear that such reports were the subject of Tajfun's, and later Sigma's, interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is my proposition, that they did not report about any kind of corruption before we had banned them all together. We don't have time to prove it today, but does this sound acceptable and reasonable to you, that first they were banned at a very early stage. First, they were ordered to -- their reintegration was ordered, and then they were banned, and it was only afterwards that they wanted to ingratiate themselves with the political leadership of Serbia. And do you remember at the time our relations with the political leadership of Serbia were very bad and they wanted to ingratiate themselves on that basis with the Serbian leadership?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I find your explanation of the sequence of events somewhat plausible, however, I do not personally have the knowledge. I would have to review all the documents of Tajfun and Sigma again to make a finding analytically as to when they first began reporting on allegations of corruption, but I certainly agree with you that Sigma came about at a time when the political leadership of Serbia was -- and its relations with the leadership of the Bosnian Serb Republic were very bad, and I think that the leadership of Slobodan Milosevic at that time was very interested in collecting material that could be used to put pressure on the Bosnian Serb leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Nielsen. Please do not feel offended in any way. I was just attacking a lack of precision, not you in any way. If curiosity killed the cat, imprecision killed the truth. Do you agree with that? Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Doctor, and I thank you for the many questions you put to me. It was my pleasure to answer your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karadzic. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, the first matter I want to deal with isn't strictly a matter of re-examination. I simply want to clear up the confusion which occurred in relation to one of the log-books, and I have the log-book from the evidence unit. Dr. Nielsen did say that he wanted to take a look at the entire log-book, and if I may do that. That's in relation to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That's at transcript pages 16332 to 16333, and it's in relation to the exhibit which was marked MFI P2991. Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Dr. Nielsen, you recall that I asked you if you had reviewed the entries from the 9th to the 16th of July 1995 and you confirmed that you had. I asked you if the log-book then showed that communications were being sent between the IDB and other organs in the RS, the RSK and Serbia during this period and you confirmed that it was consistent with communications functioning among the institutions. You then said, and I quote: "In this case, I believe if I'm not mistaken that this is a log-book of incoming dispatches." And then you went on to say that you would need to review the entire book. I'd ask you to go to the entries which we began discussing last week, and that's on ERN -- starts on the ERN page 0310326. Sorry, 3 -- 0371-0323 were the beginning of the entries that we were discussing. Do you see the sequential numbering in column 4 of the document? And this can come up in e-court so Your Honours can see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you can upload it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's 65 ter number -- --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it's coming.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I see the sequential numbering in column 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And would that indicate to you whether this was a log-book of incoming or dispatches or communications being sent?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the case of this log-book, when I'm looking now at both pages in front of me, I see both documents that are being logged here as being from some other sources and there's also documents that are being logged here as being for some sources. In any case, it's to me concurrent with the fact -- and I would note that besides this log-book, I'm familiar with a great many log-books of a similar nature covering this period that I was able to review documentation, including this log-book that showed that both incoming and outgoing communications were occurring regularly during this period in July 1995 involving the RS MUP and its various constituent units as well as government organs and relevant units of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the other log-book that we saw last Thursday was Exhibit MFI P2990, which you confirmed were the outgoing -- the -- the communications being received, did you not?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What does this last column say, receiver's signature?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, unfortunately in relation to the English translation, originally we had just the headings of the -- the 65 ter number done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm asking the witness, because he's aware of -- he speaks the language. But I think --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, can I just say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm wondering whether this is not something that parties can agree when this is log-book received or received for --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just say we have to revise this English translation though, because when the translators did these excerpts that we asked them to do, they then did the incorrect headings, because you can -- if you can see in the log-book, the date and the time, columns 2 and 3, are separate columns, and here they've given one column as column 2. And then you will also see over columns 10 and 11 are also given only one column in this English translation column 9, and it should be columns 10 and 11. So there should be 12 columns in the English translation. There's only 10. So we are having that revised. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And how should this be translated? "Potpis primaoca."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I agree that the English translation of column -- what is column 12, the far right-hand column in this log-book, "potpis primaoca" is the recipient's signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please consider whether this is something easily agreed upon on the part of the Defence. Let's move on, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Dr. Nielsen, yesterday at transcript pages 16459 to 164 -- I'm sorry. Before I do that, Your Honour, can I ask that the MFI status be removed from -- from P2990 and P2991. Obviously pending the -- as long as we get the correct translation, English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you remind me again? What was the reason for marking for identification?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Because we were -- because we were just getting the entries, the full entries from both of the log-books that I took Dr. Nielsen to for the periods between the 9th and the -- and the 16th of July. And on the other log-book, a similar date range. So that's why they were marked for identification last Thursday. I'm asking them -- for the MFI to be removed and for them to be fully admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then that will be done.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay. Dr. Nielsen, as I said, yesterday at transcript page 16459 to 16462, Mr. Karadzic asked you about the process of conferring awards on members of the MUP. He showed you a couple of documents. I want to show you two MUP documents and ask your views on the awards mentioned in those documents and the first one is 65 ter 23195. This is a proposal dated the 7th of August, 1995. Who is it from?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is type-signed by the leader of the State Security Service of the RS, Dragan Kijac. I would note that it is not signed by him but has been signed for him. It may well be actually -- the signature might be Skipina, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And it's addressed to the deputy minister, and again to remind the Chamber, who is the deputy minister in August 1995?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tomislav Kovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what's being proposed and why?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The State Security Service is nominating employees of its regional centre of state security in Bijeljina for -- and specifically is offering them a kind of monetary award for actions that they undertook in what is referred to as the liberation of Zepa and Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And was it common to request that MUP members be awarded money rather than a promotion in rank or a decoration?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that for the period of 1992, I'm not aware of monetary awards of this kind. It may have been the case that such awards were made in 1995. I do know that there are cases in which particularly deserving members of the police, again seen with the eyes of the ministry, would be nominated to receive, among other things, larger apartments or other types of non-monetary compensation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I object to this. I think this did not really arise from the direct examination. This is an attempt for the Prosecution to show that people rewarded who participated in the Srebrenica event and those events were not the subject of any of the cross-examination and I don't think it's right to admit the document at this stage through this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I hear from you, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Karadzic discussed with the witness the process of conferring the awards on members of the MUP, and this is another example of how awards were conferred.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I kindly ask for just one clarification. I spoke about proposals made to the president of the republic to confer decorations, whereas this is an internal matter of the MUP, intelligence officers at that, who did not take part in combat, who were just providing information. This has nothing to do with the president.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber finds it difficult to see that this question has arisen from the cross-examination, so we'll not admit this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Dr. Nielsen, during the discussion about the Wolves of Vucjak, you noted and this is at transcript page 16417, a report by Zupljanin in September of 1991 regarding this group. If I could 65 ter number 00906 on the screen, please. And if we could have page 3 of e-court, which is page 1 the report. Is this the report that you were referring to? And if I could draw your attention to the last paragraph on page 1, on the first page of this report. Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure, because do I not in this -- I know that the report was from Banja Luka in September 1991, but in the Serbian language here which I'm looking at, I don't yet see the passage to which I referred the Court's attention yesterday when we had it up during cross-examination where there was a reference to specifically to Mr. Milankovic. Now I see a reference to him. If I could also have the next page in Serbian, please. It may be the case that there's an additional document. This is one of the documents certainly sent during this period showing an awareness by Zupljanin and CSB Banja Luka of who Veljko Milankovic was and what kind of background he had. The document we had up yesterday, which may have been a different one, specifically referred to 54 criminal complaints that were pending against Mr. Milankovic at this same period.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You were asked about -- Mr. Karadzic put to you that -- that the Wolves of Vucjak were resubordinated to the VRS and that they were good fighters and that they did not commit any crimes.
